pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–9 years

- **Topic:** Vibrations & Sound

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 4 Science, Sound):** identify how sounds are made, associating some of them with something vibrating; recognise that vibrations from sounds travel through a medium to the ear.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 1-PS4-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-1]. (Clarification: vibrating materials that make sound include tuning forks and a plucked stretched string; sound making matter vibrate includes paper held near a speaker or an object near a vibrating tuning fork.)

- **Operational details:** The aim is the GENERAL idea that all sounds are produced by vibration — both directions of 1-PS4-1: vibration makes sound, and sound makes things vibrate. Run a recurring "spot the vibration" routine: for every new sound, ask what is vibrating. Crucially, include sources where the vibration is NOT obvious (a struck wooden block, two clinked stones, a wind instrument) alongside obvious ones (drum, plucked string), because where the vibration is hidden children abandon the idea and invent human-action explanations ('the bang is because you hit it hard'). Make invisible vibrations visible or felt: rice/grains bouncing on a drum skin, a tuning fork dipped in water or touched to the cheek, a finger on the throat while humming, paper fluttering near a speaker (the sound-makes-things-vibrate direction). Keep it concrete — avoid the sound-wave abstraction and the oscilloscope at this stage. Have children draw how they think sound is made/travels and revisit those diagrams as ideas develop.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 6–9 this is a concrete, evidence-based achievement: the child investigates and concludes that vibrating things make sound and that sound can make things vibrate. The threshold is generalising from visibly-vibrating instruments to ALL sound sources — surfacing and overturning the 'it just makes a noise / you caused it by hitting it' explanation by hunting down the hidden vibration. The medium-to-the-ear and pitch/volume relationships are adjacent Year 4 ideas built on this foundation.
bestPractices: Run a recurring 'spot the vibration' routine: for every sound, ask and find what is vibrating, so children build the general rule that ALL sound comes from vibration.

Deliberately include sources where the vibration is NOT obvious (struck block, clinked stones, wind instrument) alongside obvious ones (drum, plucked string) — hidden vibrations are exactly where children revert to 'you made the noise by hitting it'.
Make invisible vibrations visible or felt: rice/grains on a drum skin, a tuning fork in water or against the cheek, a finger on the throat while humming.
Teach BOTH directions: not only that vibration makes sound, but that sound makes things vibrate (paper fluttering by a speaker; a tuning fork splashing water) — the second half of 1-PS4-1.
Keep it concrete: avoid introducing the sound-wave diagram or oscilloscope at this stage; those abstractions come later.

Have children draw how they think a sound is made and travels, then revisit and amend the diagrams as understanding grows; use diagnostic questions to surface the 'no visible vibration' and 'sound as substance' ideas.
keyRepresentations: Rice, salt or a light ball bouncing on a drum skin (vibration made visible)
A tuning fork — dipped in water (splashes), touched to the cheek (felt), held against a table (heard louder)
A plucked stretched elastic band or guitar string blurring into visible to-and-fro
Finger on the throat / larynx while humming or speaking
Paper or a light flag fluttering in front of a speaker (sound → vibration direction)
commonMisconceptions: Only things you can SEE vibrating make sound; where no vibration is visible the sound must come from something else (usually 'because you hit it / blew it').
Sound is a kind of substance or particle, and different sounds are made of different kinds of stuff.
A sound is explained by the material ('it's metal') rather than by the act of vibrating.
Vibration makes sound, but sound cannot make things vibrate (missing the reverse direction).
Sound travels only in a straight line to the listener's ear, rather than spreading out (a foundation-stage seed of a later misconception).

learn.summary: For ages 6–9, help children reach the general idea that ALL sounds are produced by vibration — including both directions of the concept: vibrating things make sound, and sound can make things vibrate. The core challenge is generalising from obviously-vibrating sources (drum, plucked string) to sources where the vibration is hidden (struck wooden block, clinked stones, wind instrument), where children tend to abandon the vibration idea and substitute a human-action explanation ('the bang is just because you hit it hard'). Run a recurring 'spot the vibration' routine: for each sound, hunt down what is vibrating, making invisible vibrations visible or felt. Keep it concrete — avoid the sound-wave diagram and oscilloscope at this stage.

activities.title: Spot the vibration: a hunt across sound-makers
feedback: If a child says a still-looking block has 'no vibration — the sound just came from hitting it hard', invite them to touch it straight after striking to feel the brief buzz, then compare it with sources whose vibration is easier to reveal (grains on a drum skin, a tuning fork dipped in water), explaining that the block's wobble is tiny and fades fast but is there while it sounds.

If a child agrees for a visible string but doubts a hidden source, ask: 'is something vibrating in BOTH the wobbling guitar string AND the triangle you can't see move? How could we show it for the triangle?'
Praise naming the specific vibrating part (drum skin, string, voice box) rather than just saying 'it makes a noise'.
activities.rationale: Hidden-vibration sources are exactly where children revert to human-action explanations, so deliberately pairing obvious and non-obvious sources and revealing the hidden motion targets the misconception directly. Making vibration visible or felt gives concrete evidence a 'still' object is actually moving.
sourceClaims: Misconception that sound is made by vibrations only where vibrations can be seen, so children invent another (often human-action) mechanism for non-obvious sources; some treat sound as a substance/particle and different sounds as different matter; learning challenge is the general idea that all sounds are produced by vibration; 'spot the vibration' teaching approach.

Oak teaching guidance: deliberately include sounds from non-obvious vibrating sources (e.g. a string, wind instrument, two stones); the sound-wave/oscilloscope abstraction is avoided at the introductory stage and developed later; children draw and revisit how they think sound travels.
learnerActions: Make a sound with an obviously-vibrating source and find the vibration: tap a drum with grains of rice or salt resting on the skin and watch them leap and skitter; pluck a stretched elastic band or guitar string and watch it blur into visible to-and-fro.
Hum or speak with your fingers gently on your throat; describe the buzz you feel and say where the sound comes from.
Now try a source that looks perfectly still — a struck wooden block, two clinked stones, a recorder or other wind instrument. Before testing, say whether you think anything is vibrating.

Hunt for the hidden vibration in more than one way, choosing a method that suits the source: touch the struck block or stones straight after striking to try to feel a brief buzz (it fades quickly, so it may be faint); rest light grains on a sounding object and watch whether they bounce; for a recorder or other wind instrument, remember the main vibrating part is the air inside, so rest your fingers lightly on the instrument while it plays and notice the sound stops when the blowing stops; dip a sounding tuning fork in water to see it splash; touch a sounding tuning fork gently to your cheek to feel it; or hold its base against a table to hear it louder.
For each source, place or say a 'what's vibrating?' tag naming the part that moves (for a wind instrument, the air inside it).
Draw how you think a sound is made and travels; revisit and amend your drawing as your ideas develop.
activities.intendedInsight: Every sound is made by something vibrating — even when the movement is too small or too fast to see, and in a wind instrument the main vibrating thing is the air inside. Depending on the source, the vibration can sometimes be revealed by feeling a buzz, by light grains that bounce, or (for a tuning fork) by splashing water.

activities.title: The reverse direction: sound makes things vibrate
feedback: If a child doubts the rice will jump from sound alone, have them predict then test, and notice the rice moving without anything touching or blowing on it.
If a child says 'only vibrating things make sound — a sound can't make anything else vibrate', point to the fluttering paper and jumping rice as evidence the link runs both ways.
Connect back: the sound travelling through the air sets the drum skin (and the rice resting on it) or the paper moving — that is sound making matter vibrate.
activities.rationale: The sound-makes-matter-vibrate direction is the second half of the target standard and is easily forgotten; a predict–test task with rice on a drum (shouting, not touching) and paper at a speaker provides direct observable evidence of it.
sourceClaims: NGSS 1-PS4-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-1]'; clarification names tuning forks, plucked stretched string, and paper near a speaker.
learnerActions: Rest a few grains of rice on a drum skin. Predict what will happen to the rice when you shout right next to the drum (without touching it) — and say why before you try.
Play a loud, low sound from a speaker near the drum, or shout beside it without touching or blowing on it, and watch whether the rice jumps (the sound may need to be loud and close).
Hold a light paper flag or small strip of paper in front of a speaker playing a loud, low sound; watch whether it flutters, and compare with the speaker switched off.
Explain what pushed the rice / fluttered the paper, and what this shows about sound.
activities.intendedInsight: Sound carries energy that can shake things, so the link runs both ways: vibration makes sound, and sound makes matter vibrate.

activities.title: Check: hidden vibration and reverse direction
feedback: Full grasp: states sound is always caused by vibration even when too fast/small to see, AND that sound can make things vibrate, and proposes a suitable way to reveal a hidden vibration (touch to feel the buzz, rest light grains on it, or, for a tuning fork, dip it in water).
Partial: agrees for visible cases (string, drum skin) but doubts hidden ones, or omits the reverse direction — return to the hidden-vibration hunt and the rice-on-a-drum demonstration.

Gap: denies vibration whenever it is invisible and credits the hitting/blowing, or treats sound as a substance emitted from the object — reframe sound as a vibration passed along through the air, not stuff that leaves the object; the object loses no material, and its vibration simply dies away.
activities.rationale: When vibration is visible most children readily agree it makes the sound; a prompt built on a HIDDEN vibration where 'you hit it hard' competes discriminates genuine understanding from the misconception. A matching or true/false check can confirm the conclusion and classification but does not itself elicit the hands-on discovery, so pair it with the investigation that produces the evidence.
sourceClaims: Misconception that sound is made by vibrations only where vibrations can be seen, so children invent another (often human-action) mechanism for non-obvious sources; some treat sound as a substance/particle and different sounds as different matter; learning challenge is the general idea that all sounds are produced by vibration; 'spot the vibration' teaching approach.
learnerActions: Consider: 'You tap a solid wooden block and it makes a sound, but you can't SEE it moving at all. Your friend says the sound is just because you hit it hard — nothing is vibrating. What do you really think is happening, and how could we check?'
State whether something is vibrating and propose a concrete way to reveal the hidden vibration.
Match several sources to what is vibrating in each, including at least one where the vibration is invisible.
Decide, with reasons, whether this statement is right: 'A sound can make something else vibrate.'
activities.intendedInsight: A secure understanding insists there must be a hidden vibration even in a still-looking block, proposes a way to reveal it, and accepts that sound can make things vibrate too.

constraints: Keep it concrete at this stage: avoid introducing the sound-wave diagram or the oscilloscope; those abstractions are developed later.

Deliberately include sources where the vibration is NOT obvious (struck block, clinked stones, wind instrument) alongside obvious ones — omitting hidden-vibration cases leaves the misconception untouched.

Teach BOTH directions: vibration makes sound AND sound makes things vibrate; keep the reverse-direction examples clean (sound making SEPARATE matter move, e.g. shouting near rice without touching, or paper near a speaker) and do not label a tuning fork splashing its own water as the reverse direction.

Matching, true/false and multiple-choice tasks can check the conclusion and classification, but they do not themselves elicit the hands-on discovery; use investigation (feeling the buzz, seeing grains bounce, splashing water) to generate the evidence.

A static image cannot depict the to-and-fro motion, and being told that an object vibrates is not the same as seeing or feeling it move; use real, amplified or slow-motion motion, feeling, or light grains so children see or feel that a 'still-looking' object is actually moving.
The medium-to-the-ear and pitch/volume relationships are adjacent Year 4 ideas that build on this foundation, not part of this objective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (Oak National Academy guidance) was marked verified:false in the original row; treat its claims as unverified.

The original artefact-fit notes asserted a static image 'cannot show the oscillation' and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these are comparative/preference claims not established by the sources, so they are retained only as narrowly-scoped affordance/limit statements, not universal laws.
When using a predict–test with shouting near a drum, ensure the child does not touch the drum, so the observed rice movement is attributable to sound rather than contact.

The original recommendation listed a tuning fork splashing water as a reverse-direction (sound→matter) example; this is more accurately the fork's own vibration made visible by contact with the water, so it is used only in the hidden-vibration hunt, not as evidence of sound making separate matter vibrate.

assess.poeTask: Rest a few grains of rice on a drum skin. Predict what will happen to the rice when you bang the drum (or shout right next to it) — and say why before you try. Then do it and explain what it shows about vibration and sound.
probeDeeper: Put your fingers gently on your throat and hum — what do you feel, and what does it tell you about where the sound comes from?
When you shout right next to a drum with rice on it, the rice jumps. What is pushing the rice?
A guitar string you can see wobbling, and a triangle you can't — is something vibrating in BOTH? How could you show it for the triangle?
assess.correctAnswer: The block IS vibrating — moving back and forth very fast, too small to see — and that vibration is what makes the sound. We could check by touching it to feel the buzz, or by resting light grains on it (or dipping it in water) to reveal the wobble.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sound needs a visible vibration, so a hidden one is denied: 'there's no vibration, the sound came from hitting it hard' — the tell is 'I can't see it move so nothing moved'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a recurring 'spot the vibration' routine; make invisible vibrations visible or felt (rice on a drum, tuning fork dipped in water, fingers on the throat); deliberately choose non-obvious sound sources.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's no vibration — the sound just comes from hitting the block hard.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies vibration in a struck block, clinked stones, or a wind instrument; credits the human action instead

errorPatterns.pattern: Sound as a substance: 'sound is a stuff that comes out of it, and different sounds are different stuff'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe sound as a vibration that is passed along, not matter that leaves the object; nothing is 'used up' or emitted as a substance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about sound as a material emitted and travelling out, rather than as a vibration passed on

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgetting the reverse direction: 'vibrating things make sound, but a sound can't make something else vibrate'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rice-on-a-drum or a paper flag on a speaker cone — sound carries energy that shakes things; the link runs both ways.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only vibrating things make sound; a sound can't make anything else vibrate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts vibration-to-sound but denies sound-to-vibration (e.g. doubts that rice will jump when you shout near a drum)

responseLevels.gap: Denies vibration whenever it is invisible and credits the hitting/blowing, or treats sound as a substance that is emitted.
responseLevels.full: States that sound is always caused by vibration — even when too fast or small to see — AND that sound can make things vibrate; proposes a way to reveal a hidden vibration, transferring across visible and hidden sources.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees that vibrating objects make sound for VISIBLE cases (string, drum skin) but doubts it for hidden ones, or omits the reverse direction (sound making things vibrate).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You tap a solid wooden block and it makes a sound, but you can't SEE it moving at all. Your friend says 'the sound is just because you hit it hard — nothing is vibrating.' What do you think is really happening, and how could we check?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: When the vibration is visible (a plucked guitar string) every child agrees it makes the sound. This prompt uses a HIDDEN vibration (a struck solid block) where the intuitive 'you hit it hard' cause competes. A child who genuinely holds 'sound = vibration' insists there must be a hidden vibration and proposes a way to reveal it; the misconception child denies any vibration and credits the hitting.
